questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of substernal chest pain. He described it as burning and associated with swallowing solids and liquids. He had not had any vomiting, diarrhea, or blood in his stools. He was known to have HIV and intermittently took his antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis treatments. On oral examination there were white mucosal plaque lesions that easily scraped off but no ulcerations. Investigations: CD4 count 65 cells/μ L HIV-1 RNA viral load 22,150 copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Fluconazole The patient’s presentation with clinical symptoms suggestive of esophagitis and oral candidiasis (thrush) is most consistent with candida esophagitis, which is treated with fluconazole. Nystatin would be inadequate for esophageal involvement. Herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus can also cause esophagitis but would be less common, particularly given the concomitant thrush. Pantoprazole, used for reflux esophagitis, would be a diagnosis of exclusion after infectious causes were ruled out.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q37

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man was reviewed with a 4-day history of fevers and hypotension despite empiric use of broadspectrum antibiotics. The man had presented to hospital 3 weeks earlier with profuse diarrhea and severe malnutrition. He had Crohn’s disease with short gut syndrome secondary to multiple bowel resections. He was initiated at admission on total parenteral nutrition via central venous catheter. His antimicrobials were changed to meropenem and micafungin. Investigations: Total white cell count 20 ×109/L Platelet count 50 ×109/L Blood cultures (central and peripheral) no growth after 3 days CXR: bilateral airspace disease
questions.lead_in: What is the best next test to secure a diagnosis?

options.text: Blood culture inoculated onto Sabouraud dextrose agar
Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil

questions.explanation: Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil This is a case of disseminated Malassezia infection. Risk factors in this case include CVC and lipid infusions (TPN). Malassezia spp. are intrinsically resistant to echinocandins, thus a response to micafungin is not expected. Malassezia spp. are lipophilic, and all species but M. pachydermatis require exogenous lipids for growth. M. furfur is the most common pathogen involved in disseminated disease. Recovery from standard blood cultures is low unless the media is enriched with fatty acids, i.e., with olive oil, palmitic acid, Tween, etc., or with Dixon’s agar, which contains glycerol mono-oleate. Serum 1,3- β-D-glucan is a nonspecific biomarker of fungal disease. It is not particularly helpful in making a diagnosis. Panfungal PCR is not useful on blood because of the low burden of organisms in the total circulation. Serum CrAg is used for the diagnosis of cryptococcosis (including subclinical disease). It also can cross react with Trichosporon spp. in disseminated disease, although a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis. Trichosporonosis has been reported in neonates but is less likely than Malassezia disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q26

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman presented for routine clinic review. She had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and was 4 years postrenal transplant. She denied urinary frequency, dysuria, or focal symptoms. Her graft function was excellent. Investigations: Urine microscopy: 30 leucocytes per high-powered field Urine culture: pure heavy growth of Candida species
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Reassurance only There is no indication to treat asymptomatic candiduria in this clinical context. Pyuria is not an indication for treatment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q21

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with a 5-week history of throat pain and difficulty swallowing. The odynophagia had worsened over time, limiting oral intake. He had had a negative rapid strep test and a 2-week course of penicillin without symptomatic response. He had 1 week of night sweats but no fever or chills. He had a dry cough for 2 weeks but no dyspnea. He had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and had renal transplantation 18 months prior. He had been born and brought up in Indonesia and had come to the United States for college. He had been screened for TB 4 years earlier and had had a chest X-ray then which showed a small linear opacity in the right lower lobe. Tuberculosis skin and sputum testing at that time was negative. Current medications included prednisone 7.5 mg daily, mycophenolate 1 gram twice daily, and tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily. On examination his temperature was 98.2°F. Tonsils and posterior pharynx were inflamed and erythematous. There were no exudates or other lesions. There were no other abnormalities on exam. Investigations: CXR: right lower lobe density with calcification, unchanged from previous films HIV antibody, CMV viral load, and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis were negative CT scan of the neck: thickening of the epiglottis and left piriform sinus On endoscopy, the true vocal cords were normal in appearance. The epiglottis was thickened and the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis and supraglottic folds had irregular white friable tissue.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis The patient presents with a chronic epiglottitis, on a background of immunocompromise due to immunosuppression for renal transplantation. Granulomatous diseases and malignancy must be considered in the differential diagnosis. Due to the patient’s history of being born in Indonesia, along with the radiographic abnormalities, tuberculosis is the likely diagnosis in this case.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q6

questions.stem: A 35-year-old developed fungemia with Candida parapsilosis during a prolonged hospital course in the ICU with nonischemic heart failure. Her central lines were removed, surveillance cultures were negative, and echocardiogram was unrevealing. She was treated initially with caspofungin followed by fluconazole once speciation and sensitivities returned. Two weeks later, she lost vision in her right eye. Dilated eye exam revealed fluffy vitreal lesions. She had an urgent vitrectomy with intravitreal antifungal injection.
questions.lead_in: What systemic agent would be preferred for treatment?
questions.explanation: Voriconazole Voriconazole or fluconazole would be the best option as they penetrate the eye well, unless there are concerns for resistance. Her case is describing the natural course of endophthalmitis rather than treatment failure, and C. parapsilosis should be azole-sensitive. While amphotericin will penetrate the eye, she could avoid the toxicity by using an azole. The echinocandins have very poor penetration into the eye.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q10

needs: Chapter 310 — Infections in the Immunocompromised Host
questions.stem: A 19-year-old man was diagnosed with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) after recurrent infections from the age of 5 years old. Hypoparathyroidism was diagnosed after an episode of tetanic spasms at 10 years old. At 15 years of age, he developed adrenal insufficiency.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in the IL-17 axis

questions.explanation: APECED syndrome Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy–Candidiasis–Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED) or autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 is characterized by the triad of CMC, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease. CARD9 deficiency and IL-17 deficiencies can also present with CMC but lack the endocrinopathies. Patients with MCM4 deficiency, on the other hand, also present with adrenal insufficiency, while patients with DiGeorge syndrome also have hypoparathyroidism.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q26

questions.question: A woman who was previously treated at another hospital presents with fever and sepsis with a central line. Blood culture is positive at 6 hours with a yeast-like organism.

parts.text: What is your next management steps for the catheter and for antimicrobial treatment?
Name a test to differentiate albicans vs non albicans, and indicate what the expected result is for C. albicans.
The isolate is non-albicans. Do you change anything in your management, and if so, what?

The candida is identified as C. haemulonii with high MIC to azoles, echinocandins and amphotericin. However, you do not believe this result. What do you suspect? Are there any special precautions to take?

questions.model_answer: a) Catheter management: remove the central line promptly (source control - candidemia mandates catheter removal); start empiric antifungal therapy immediately, do not wait for speciation. Antimicrobial: empiric echinocandin (e.g. caspofungin or micafungin) pending speciation/susceptibilities. b) Test to differentiate C. albicans from non-albicans: germ tube test - C. albicans is germ tube positive (forms a germ tube when incubated in serum at 37°C), whereas most non-albicans species are germ tube negative. c) If non-albicans: reassess antifungal choice based on species and susceptibility (e.g. C. glabrata/C. krusei have reduced fluconazole susceptibility - continue echinocandin; C. parapsilosis has relatively higher echinocandin MICs - consider fluconazole if susceptible); continue source control and ophthalmologic exam, echocardiogram if indicated for all candidemia regardless of species. d) Suspect laboratory misidentification of Candida auris (frequently misidentified as C. haemulonii by conventional biochemical/VITEK systems); given pan-resistant profile, confirm identification with MALDI-TOF or molecular sequencing. Special precautions: implement contact precautions and single-room isolation, notify infection control/public health (C. auris is a reportable, outbreak-prone organism), enhanced environmental cleaning given its ability to persist on surfaces and colonize skin.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC C. auris identification and infection control guidance

questions.question: 15. 30F with AML with central line develops fever post-chemotherapy. Blood cultures grow yeast. Microbiology lab has difficulty identifying the yeast, but it eventually is speciated to Candida auris.

parts.text: a) Which identification method reliably is able to identify C. auris?
b) Name two other Candida that can be mistaken for C. auris?
c) What is the treatment for this patient?

cohort_answer.text: Identification: PCR (D1-D2 or ITS sequencing of 28s rDNA) or MALDI-TOF. Similar species: C. haemulonii; also C. famata, C. sake, Rhodotorula glutinis, Rhodotorula mucilaginosa, Saccharomyces species; rarely C. catenulata, C. lusitaniae, C. guilliermondii, C. parapsilosis. Treatment: Remove line; initial caspofungin (load 70mg IV then 50mg IV daily) or micafungin 100mg IV daily; switch to liposomal ampho B 5mg/kg/day if clinically unresponsive or persistent fungemia >5 days (90% resistance to fluc, 30% to ampho, 5% echinocandins)

questions.question: Ex 24 weeker, now 4 weeks old. BW 800g. Septic needing reintubation. Has PICC. UC growing C. albicans

parts.text: What 3 investigations do you do?
What tx do you initate
Why did you choose that tx
What other intervention (aside from further investigations) do you need to do?

questions.model_answer: a) Three investigations: (1) Blood cultures (rule out candidemia/dissemination). (2) Ophthalmologic exam (dilated fundoscopy for chorioretinitis/endophthalmitis). (3) Renal/abdominal ultrasound (assess for fungal balls in urinary tract given candiduria) plus consider lumbar puncture and echocardiogram given risk of disseminated disease in extremely low birth weight neonate. b) Treatment: amphotericin B (conventional deoxycholate, preferred in neonates due to excellent tissue penetration including CNS/urinary tract and established safety data) - or fluconazole if susceptible and stable. c) Rationale: neonates, especially extremely preterm/ELBW infants, have immature renal/hepatic clearance and amphotericin B deoxycholate achieves good CNS and urinary tract penetration with a favorable safety profile in this population; echinocandins have limited CNS penetration and less neonatal data. d) Other intervention: remove/exchange the PICC line (source control), as with any invasive candidiasis in a patient with an indwelling catheter.

questions.question: Adult: IVDU, haemodyn stable, comes in with fevers, BC: C. albicans, ECHO: vege 7mm on post mitral valve

parts.text: 2 Initial tx regimen for this pt
2 tests to do

questions.model_answer:
a) Initial treatment regimen for Candida albicans native mitral valve IE in a hemodynamically stable patient: liposomal amphotericin B (with or without flucytosine) OR high-dose echinocandin (e.g., micafungin) as initial induction therapy, with early cardiothoracic surgical consultation for valve replacement.
b) Two additional tests: (1) Formal ophthalmologic examination to rule out endogenous Candida endophthalmitis/chorioretinitis. (2) Follow-up (surveillance) blood cultures to document clearance of candidemia, and consider transesophageal echocardiogram to better characterize the vegetation and assess for abscess/embolic risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2016 Candidiasis Guidelines for treatment of Candida endocarditis.

questions.question: PWID has fever, sweats, weight loss. Blood cultures grow C. albicans in multiple cultures and echocardiogram demonstrates a 7 mm mitral vegetation. You diagnose her with endocarditis – (2016; 2019)

parts.text: A) What test would you order next (2016)
B) What are two potential therapeutic regimens you can use?
C) Other than surgery, what are two other interventions you will advocate for?
D) Other than fungal endocarditis, name 5 other indications for early surgery

cohort_answer.text: Next test: TEE. Therapeutic regimens: Liposomal Amphotericin B +/- flucytosine; High dose echinocandin. Also: Optho consult to R/O endophthalmitis; consideration of lifelong azole suppressive therapy (even with surgical intervention per AHA 2015 IE guidelines). Other interventions: Harm reduction for safe injection/naloxone/clean supplies; Addictions consultation. Other indications for early valve surgery: S aureus and MDR gram negatives; Heart block; Heart failure due to valve dysfunction; Abscess/fistula; Fever or blood culture positive 5-7 days on appropriate therapy; Recurrent embolic phenomenon with persisting or enlarging vegetations on appropriate therapy; Severe valve regurg and vegetation over 1cm

questions.question: 21. Man from the NY State, transferred to you. Has 2 blood cultures positive for C. haemulonii.

parts.text: What is your concern about the organism?
What is the percentage of resistance for each drug? (Fluconazole, Amphotericin B, Echinocandin)
Name 3 other steps in care other than therapeutic or diagnostic

questions.model_answer: a) Concern: high likelihood this represents Candida auris misidentified as C. haemulonii (common misidentification by biochemical/VITEK-2 systems), especially given NY State association with known C. auris outbreaks - concern for multidrug resistance and healthcare transmission. b) Approximate resistance rates for C. auris: fluconazole ~90% resistant; amphotericin B ~30-40% resistant; echinocandins ~5% resistant (echinocandins generally still most reliably active, used as first-line empiric therapy). c) Three additional care steps (non-diagnostic/therapeutic): (1) Contact precautions/single-room isolation. (2) Notify infection prevention and control/public health (reportable organism, outbreak investigation). (3) Enhanced terminal cleaning/disinfection of the room and screening of close contacts/roommates for colonization.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Candida auris antifungal resistance and infection control data

questions.question: AML patient presents in septic shock. Preliminary cultures show a yeast-like organism.

parts.text: How would you treat the patient?
Cultures isolate candida species? Would you change your management?
What is 1-way to determine if this is an albicans species?
How do you interpret the test?
Candida haemulonii is isolated which is pan resistant and you don't buy it. What other species could this be?

cohort_answer.text: Echinocandin (pull lines out, repeat cultures, eye exam, +/- echo). Caspofungin: loading dose 70 mg, then 50 mg daily; micafungin: 100 mg daily; anidulafungin: loading dose 200 mg, then 100 mg daily - recommended as initial therapy per IDSA guidelines. || No, would not change management. || Germ tube test. || Difference is albicans makes germ tubes but others make pseudohyphae: a) germ tube b) pseudohyphae. || C. auris.

questions.question: C. albicans

parts.text: What is the rapid test for it?
How do you interpret it?

cohort_answer.text: Test: Germ tube test. Interpretation: Screening test to differentiate Candida albicans from other yeast; grown in human/sheep serum at 37°C for 3 hours, forms germ tube detected via wet KOH films as filamentous outgrowth; positive for Candida albicans and Candida dubliniensis. Minimum 5 germ tubes should be observed before calling positive. Growth at 45°C separates C. albicans from C. dubliniensis.

questions.question: Preterm infant in NICU with necrotizing enterocolitis, and has PICC line. BCx and Urine Cx are growing C. albicans while on fluconazole prophylaxis.

parts.text: What antifungal agent should you treat with?
What are 3 guideline-based (IDSA) reasons to start this drug?
What other interventions are required?

cohort_answer.text: Agent: AmB deoxycholate 1mg/kg daily (preferred in disseminated candidiasis in neonates; lipid AmB has poor urine penetration; fluconazole avoided due to prophylaxis failure/resistance concern; echinocandins limited data in neonates, poor urine/CNS penetration). Reasons: well-tolerated and less nephrotoxic in neonates; AmB-deoxycholate associated with better outcomes/lower mortality; these infants at high risk for CNS involvement. Other interventions: Remove CVC regardless of neutropenia status; lumbar puncture to assess for meningitis; dilated retinal exam; consider CT/US of GU/liver/spleen if persistent positive; repeat blood cultures daily/every other day (echo not needed)

questions.question: Female PWID with C. albicans fungemia and native MV IE (vegetation 7mm).

parts.text: Name 2 antifungal regimens to treat this infection.
What are 5 indications for valve replacement?
Name two management strategies other than antifungal therapy and surgery

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: High-dose echinocandins (micafungin 150mg IV daily); Lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg +/- flucytosine 25mg/kg QID; duration 6 weeks after surgery, step down to oral fluconazole 400-800mg daily if cultures clear and susceptible. Valve replacement indications: symptomatic heart failure; challenging/highly resistant organism; infection complicated by heart block/abscess; failure to clear blood cultures (>5-7 days); MV vegetation >10mm (esp anterior leaflet); persistent vegetation after embolization. Other management: repeat blood cultures, eye exam, follow-up echo; CVC removal

questions.question: AM 5. AML patient went to New York has a CVC, was septic and hospitalized there, now presents septic again with yeast in BC after 6h

parts.text: What will you do with the central line and empiric antimicrobial treatment? (2)
What test will differentiate C. albicans vs. non-albicans? (1)
Grows a non-albicans - would you change your antimicrobial therapy and if so to what (0.5)
Grows C. haemulonii resistant to azoles and polyenes and I think echinocandins. You suspect there is an alternative explanation. What is the organism? (1)
What, if any, are the isolation precautions? (1)

cohort_answer.text: Remove central line immediately; empiric micafungin 100mg IV q24h. Germ tube test (C. albicans gets germ tube after incubation; C. dubliniensis also positive). Non-albicans - stay the same. Organism: C. auris. Isolation: Contact precautions (as for any MDR organism).

questions.question: 27. Fungal IE – C. albicans with 6mm vegetation on MV in IVDU

parts.text: Name 2 potential therapeutic regimens
Other than surgery, name 2 other interventions
5 other indications for surgery (other than fungal IE)

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: Liposomal Amphotericin B 3-5mg/kg IV daily +/- flucytosine 25mg/kg PO QID; Micafungin 150mg IV daily followed by lifelong suppression (fluconazole monotherapy for initial therapy has higher failure). Other interventions: TEE (abscess), ophthalmologic exam. Surgery indications: persistent blood culture positivity (≥7 days), vegetation ≥1cm with evidence of embolization, symptomatic heart failure, abscess, prosthetic valve.

questions.question: Gentleman is transferred from NYC and has 2 blood cultures positive for Candida haemulonii.

parts.text: What are you worried about and why?
What are the approximate resistance rates to fluconazole, amphoB, and echinocandins?
What are 3 next steps (not related to diagnosis or therapy)

cohort_answer.text: Worried about C. auris (Candida haemulonii can be misidentified as/related to C. auris). Approximate resistance rates (CDC US data): Fluconazole ~90%; L-AmphoB ~30%; Echinocandins ~5% (echinocandin best empiric treatment pending susceptibility). Next steps: Place patient on contact precautions; Contact local public health authorities and CDC; Confirm identity of Candida auris; hand hygiene. (IPC for C. auris: contact precautions, single room when possible, cleaning/disinfection with 10% bleach or EPA-approved product, screening contacts; do not do routine swabs once known positive.)

questions.question: A 500mg 25 week old boy is on Fluconazole prophylaxis in the NICU. He has a PICC line. He becomes septic.

parts.text: Based on the 2016 IDSA Guidelines which antifungal therapy is recommended first line.
What are three reasons this therapy is recommended (as per IDSA Guidelines)
In addition to investigations, what one other intervention should be performed for this boy?

cohort_answer.text:
AmpB deoxycholate 1mg/kg daily
AmB deoxycholate has better kidney penetration vs AmB liposomal; well tolerated in neonates, low nephrotoxicity; risk of fluconazole-resistant candidiasis (was on fluc ppx); neonates on liposomal AmB had higher mortality than deoxycholate/fluconazole; echinocandin concentrations low in CNS/urinary tract
PICC line removal

questions.question: 26 yo F IVDU with fever, night sweats, etc. Blood cultures x4 positive for Candida Albicans.

parts.text: What test would you order next?
What 2 therapies are first line in this condition?
What 2 interventions (management) which you would recommend for this patient?
What are 4 indications for early surgery other than fungal infection?

cohort_answer.text: TEE. First line therapies: L-AMB with or without flucytosine, or echinocandin (increased dose e.g. micafungin 150mg) for at least 6-10 weeks after surgery; can switch to fluconazole if susceptible Candida + clinically stable + cleared BCx; valve replacement/surgery should not wait; close monitoring and often fluconazole as long-term suppressive therapy. (For candidal endocarditis: AmpB+flucytosine has mortality benefit vs monotherapy, fungicidal, step down to PO fluconazole if susceptible; for candidemia, echinocandins or fluconazole appropriate first-line per IDSA 2016; lifelong suppression fluconazole 400-800mg daily if NVIE/PVIE without valve surgery.) Interventions: Early valve replacement surgery for fungal endocarditis (mortality benefit); at least 6 weeks of therapy (longer if abscess/complications), followed by lifelong azole therapy regardless of surgical status (AHA/IDSA 2015 IE guidelines - reasonable in patients post valve surgery; Candida guidelines differ, suggesting suppression only if not surgical candidate or prosthetic valve). (4 indications for early surgery other than fungal infection: not documented in source.)

questions.question: Patient from New York has blood cultures positive for Candida haemulonii.

parts.text: What are you worried about, and why do you care?
What is the approximate percentage (no acceptable range given) resistance of the suspected organism to fluconazole, amphotericin, and echinocandins?
Besides investigations and management for the patient, what are three interventions that are required?

questions.model_answer: a) Concern: likely Candida auris (frequently misidentified as C. haemulonii by standard biochemical panels), a multidrug-resistant, healthcare-associated, outbreak-prone organism with high mortality and environmental persistence - care because of transmission risk and limited treatment options. b) Approximate resistance: fluconazole ~90%; amphotericin B ~30%; echinocandins ~5%. c) Three additional interventions: (1) Contact precautions and single-room isolation. (2) Infection control/public health notification (reportable pathogen, outbreak investigation, screening of contacts). (3) Enhanced environmental cleaning/disinfection of the patient's room and equipment.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Candida auris resistance/infection control data

questions.question: You see a patient presenting with acute heart failure. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates a 1.2 cm vegetation on the aortic valve associated with severe aortic regurgitation. Blood cultures are positive for Candida albicans. Abdominal imaging demonstrates several splenic abscesses.

parts.text: List TWO antifungal agents from different classes that can be used as monotherapy.
List THREE indications this patient has for early surgery.
If the patient cannot undergo valve surgery, describe the antifungal management (based on IDSA guidelines).

questions.model_answer:
a) Two antifungal agents from different classes usable as monotherapy for Candida IE: liposomal amphotericin B (polyene) and an echinocandin (e.g., micafungin or caspofungin).
b) Three indications for early surgery in this patient: (1) severe aortic regurgitation with acute heart failure. (2) Fungal (Candida) IE, which is generally ineffectively treated with antifungals alone. (3) Evidence of embolic/metastatic disease (splenic abscesses), reflecting high embolic risk and a large (>1 cm) vegetation.
c) If the patient cannot undergo surgery, IDSA guidelines recommend long-term (often lifelong) suppressive antifungal therapy with fluconazole (if the isolate is susceptible), continued indefinitely to prevent relapse, following an initial induction course of liposomal amphotericin B (with or without flucytosine) or an echinocandin.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2016 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Candidiasis - Candida endocarditis section.

questions.question: Candida albicans.

parts.text: What is the rapid test for it
How to interpret test?

cohort_answer.text: Germ tube test. A rapid presumptive identification of C. albicans can be made by placing organism in serum and observing germ tube formation (small projections appearing within 90 min); used to differentiate C. albicans (and C. dubliniensis) from other Candida spp. Interpretation: sample placed in tube with sheep serum, incubated 2-4h, drop placed on slide with KOH prep - see filamentous outgrowth extending from yeast cells; positive germ tube test = C. albicans (or C. dubliniensis), based on non-constricted germ tube arising from yeast; false-negative and false-positive germ tube formations may occur; remainder of speciation relies on physiologic parameters rather than morphology.

questions.question: Man with repeat positive cultures of candida in urine and pyuria. Has known stone, but no obstruction.

parts.text: Would you treat
If so, with what?
What simple laboratory test distinguishes C. albicans from non-albicans?

cohort_answer.text: No treatment for asymptomatic candiduria unless high risk for dissemination (neutropenic patients, very low-birth-weight infants <1500g, patients undergoing urologic manipulation); renal transplantation no longer an absolute indication, consider case-by-case (UpToDate). Treatment: not recommended unless high-risk group; neutropenic/VLBW infants treated as for candidemia; patients undergoing urologic procedures: oral fluconazole 400mg (6mg/kg) daily OR AmB deoxycholate 0.3-0.6mg/kg daily for several days before/after procedure; for symptomatic cystitis: oral fluconazole 200mg (3mg/kg) daily x2 weeks, alternatively 1-7 days amphoB deoxycholate or flucytosine x7-10 days; if treating pyelo with amphoB can add flucytosine; do not use lipid formulations of amphoB (does not concentrate in kidney/bladder). Distinguishing test: Germ tube testing.

questions.question: A patient from New York is repatriated to your hospital. A sample from some site shows Candida haemulonii.

parts.text: What is your concern?
b. What resistance percent for fluconazole, ampho B and echinocandins?
c. Three non-treatment things to do.

cohort_answer.text: a) Misidentified C. auris. b) Fluconazole >90%; Ampho B 15-30%; Echinocandins 2-10%. c) Contact public health; contact IP&C and isolate patient + contact precautions; screen close contacts; hand hygiene and terminal cleaning.

questions.question: 27yo dude admitted for acute heart failure. Has endocarditis with a positive blood culture for C. albicans. Additionally, there is severe aortic regurgitation, heart failure, and multiple splenic lesions. The vegetation is 13mm.

parts.text: What initial empiric antifungal therapy (from 2 different classes) would you use?
What are 3 indications for urgent surgery present in this case.
He is deemed not a candidate for valvular surgery. Based on the 2016 AHA/IDSA guidelines, what is the recommended antifungal management in this case?

cohort_answer.text: Empiric therapy: Liposomal amphoB (3-5mg/kg) +/- flucytosine; High dose echinocandin. Urgent surgery indications: Fungal endocarditis; Severe heart failure with valve dysfunction; Large mobile vegetation with evidence of embolic phenomena. If not a surgical candidate: Step down therapy to fluconazole 400-800mg daily if susceptible isolates, clinical stability, and cleared bloodstream Candida; for patients who cannot undergo valve replacement, long term suppression with fluconazole 400-800mg daily if isolate susceptible; even with surgery, reasonable to consider lifelong prophylaxis due to recurrence risk

questions.question: Antifungal question

parts.text: What component of the cell-wall do azoles inhibit synthesis of?
Which antifungal agent is Pichia kudriavzevii (formerly Candida krusei) intrinsically resistant to?
A patient is infected with Candida auris. They have had no prior exposure to antifungal agents. What class of antifungals would you use empirically?
Name THREE antifungals active in the treatment of mucormycosis.

questions.model_answer:
a) Azoles inhibit synthesis of ergosterol, a key component of the fungal cell membrane (not the cell wall) - by blocking lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase.
b) Pichia kudriavzevii (Candida krusei) is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole.
c) For Candida auris with no prior antifungal exposure, empiric therapy with an echinocandin (e.g., micafungin or caspofungin) is recommended, given the high prevalence of fluconazole resistance in this species.
d) Antifungals active against mucormycosis: liposomal amphotericin B, posaconazole, and isavuconazole.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC guidance on Candida auris empiric treatment; general antifungal spectrum knowledge for mucormycosis.

questions.question: A patient is 30 days out from an allogeneic transplant which was complicated by severe candida mucositis and treated with fluconazole. Now has increasing LFTs.

parts.text: What is the probable cause?
What would you do with this patient now? Justify your answer

cohort_answer.text: A) Fluconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. DDX: hepatosplenic candidiasis (manifests at engraftment, median presentation 2-3 weeks post-HSCT if no ppx); CMV/VZV/EBV/HHV6/HSV/HBV (HSV highest risk pre-engraftment, usually on ppx); hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/VOD (elevated bili, hepatomegaly/RUQ pain, sudden weight gain, needs biopsy; risk factors liver dysfunction pre-tx, poorly matched donor, MTX for GVHD ppx); acute GVHD; other drugs (calcineurin inhibitor, methotrexate, TMP-SMX). B) CT abdomen/pelvis to work up hepatosplenic candidiasis; blood cultures for yeast; once cultures obtained, stop fluconazole, start echinocandin; if azole required use Posaconazole (reduced transaminitis); IDSA alternative: IV echinocandin or IV lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg daily; start empiric acyclovir for HSV if not on ppx; trend liver enzymes; look for non-infectious causes; consider esophageal brushings for yeast culture/sensitivity, Herpesviridae viral load.

needs: Chapter 311 — Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy in Cancer Patients
questions.question: Cancer patient with fever and no obvious source clinically or radiographically. On PipTazo. CVL and peripheral lines now growing a yeast-like organism.

parts.text: What is the source of the fever?
How would you investigate further?
Name 4 other potential sources of fever
List 4 treatments for this situation

cohort_answer.text: A) Fungemia - line associated or gut translocation (candidemia often from gut translocation rather than line, so don't always change lines if repeat culture negative). B) Repeat blood cultures from all lines; if Candida spp -> germ tube test; if Candida -> ophtho consult; abdominal imaging if source unclear; echocardiogram especially if persistently positive cultures. C) Infectious - bacterial (including abscess), viral, other fungal infection; Non-infectious - cancer, thrombosis, drug. D) Remove CVC; empiric echinocandin; stop PipTazo if not neutropenic; reduce immunosuppression if feasible. (IDSA alternatives: echinocandin, lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg daily, fluconazole 800mg loading then 400mg daily, voriconazole 400mg BID x2 doses then 200-300mg BID.)
